heading.b: Orders as to excessive increases in site fees

block.txt: The Tribunal may, on application under section 71 or 72, make any of the following orders—
an order declaring that an increase in site fees is excessive,
an order reducing the amount of the increase by a specified amount,
an order setting aside the increase,
an order that the site fees must not exceed a specified amount or specified amounts, either—
from a specified day, not being earlier than the day from which the increased site fees were payable, or
during a specified period,
an order confirming the increase on the conditions (if any) that the Tribunal considers appropriate,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.
The Tribunal may make orders applying to individual participating home owners, groups of participating home owners or all participating home owners.

An order applies to all affected home owners in the community (other than those who opt out), unless the Tribunal is satisfied there is a strong reason for making separate orders for different home owners or groups of home owners.

The Tribunal cannot make an order that would result in an increase lower than that needed to cover any actual or projected increase (established to the satisfaction of the Tribunal) in the outgoings and operating expenses for the community since the previous increase (if any) in site fees for the community.

heading.b: Matters to be considered about excessive increases

block.txt: The Tribunal may have regard to any or all of the following factors when deciding whether to make an order under section 73—
the frequency and amount of past increases in site fees for the community,
any actual or projected increase in the outgoings and operating expenses for the community as provided by the operator since the previous increase (if any) in site fees for the community,
any repairs or improvements to the community—
carried out by the operator since the previous increase (if any), or
planned by the operator for the period covered by the increase being reviewed,
the general condition of the community including its common areas,
the range and average level of site fees within the community,
the value of any improvements to the community (including common areas) paid for or carried out by home owners,
any explanation for the increase provided by the operator by notice in writing to the affected home owners,
variations in the Consumer Price Index (All Groups Index) for Sydney,
whether the increase is fair and equitable in the operation of the community,
any other matters prescribed by the regulations.

The regulations may require the Tribunal to disregard any specified matters (not being a matter referred to in subsection (1)), in any specified circumstances, when deciding whether to make an order under section 73.

heading.b: Interim order suspending increases in site fees

block.txt: The Tribunal may, if it is of the opinion that the circumstances so require, by order, suspend a requirement to pay the whole or part of an increase in site fees.

An application for an order under this section may be made by an affected home owner before, on or after making an application to the Tribunal for an order under section 73 in respect of the increase.

An application for an order under this section may be made on behalf of all the affected home owners (other than those who opt out of the application) by one or more of them appointed as the representative or representatives by the participating home owners.
An order under this section has effect for the period specified by the Tribunal, unless sooner revoked.
The Tribunal may revoke an order under this section at any time.
In this part—
embedded network has the same meaning as in the National Electricity Rules.
exempt seller has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
National Electricity Rules has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
retailer has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).

third party supplier, for a community, means a person that the operator of the community has entered into an agreement with to operate an embedded network or provide billing services, or both, for the community.

heading.b: Limit on amounts payable by home owner

block.txt: The only fees and charges that may be required or received by the operator of a community from a home owner in connection with the occupation of a residential site, or the use of any of the facilities of a community, are as follows—
site fees, including site fees payable in advance as permitted under section 57,
the cost of registering or recording the site agreement under the Real Property Act 1900 if any fixed term period exceeds 3 years,
a refundable deposit for a key or any other opening device to access the community, not exceeding $25 or another amount prescribed by the regulations,
other fees, charges and deposits required or permitted by this Act or the regulations.

The regulations may require or permit payment of fees, charges and deposits that are specified or of a kind specified by the regulations and, in particular, may (but need not) provide that they are not payable by a home owner unless required by the site agreement to be paid by the home owner.
An operator of a community must not require or permit the payment of any fee, charge or deposit from a home owner in contravention of this section.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.

heading.b: Utility charges payable to operator or third party supplier

block.txt: This section applies if—
a home owner is required, under a site agreement, to pay utility charges—
to the operator of the community or a third party supplier for the community for the use of electricity supplied to the residential site through an embedded network, or
to the operator for the use of a utility other than electricity at the residential site, or

a tenant is required, under a tenancy agreement, to pay utility charges to the operator of the community or a third party supplier for the community for the use of electricity supplied to the residential site through an embedded network.
The home owner is not required to pay the utility charges unless—
usage is separately measured or metered, and
the operator or third party supplier gives the home owner an itemised account in accordance with section 83, and
the home owner is given at least 21 days to make the payment.
The tenant is not required to pay the utility charges for the use of electricity unless—
the operator or third party supplier gives the tenant an itemised account in accordance with section 83, and
the tenant is given at least 21 days to make the payment.

See the Residential Tenancies Act 2010, section 40 and the Residential Tenancies Regulation 2019, clause 34 in relation to the metering requirements relating to a tenant’s liability to pay utility charges.

The operator or third party supplier must not charge a daily supply charge, or usage charge per kWh, for the use of electricity that is more than, respectively, the daily supply charge, or usage charge per kWh, that would be payable under the community’s comparable market offer.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.

For the purposes of subsection (4), the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal must determine the median retail market offer for residential customers for each distribution district in accordance with the regulations.

The operator must not charge an amount for the use of a utility other than electricity that is more than the amount charged by the utility service provider for the quantity of the service supplied to, or used at, the residential site.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.
The regulations may—
prescribe maximum utility charges payable to the operator of a community or a third party supplier for a community, and

make it an offence for the operator of a community or a third party supplier for a community to request or receive payment for a utility charge that is more than the relevant maximum utility charge, and
provide for discounts to daily supply charges payable for electricity if less than 60 amps is supplied to the residential site, and
provide for the publication of comparable market offers for communities.
In this section—

comparable market offer, in relation to a community, means the median retail market offer for residential customers, determined by the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal under subsection (5), for the distribution district of the community’s network service provider.
distribution district has the same meaning as in the Electricity Supply Act 1995.
market offer has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
network service provider has the same meaning as in the National Electricity Rules.
This section applies if—
electricity is supplied to residential sites in a community through an embedded network, and
the operator of the community or a third party supplier for the community sells the electricity to home owners or tenants, or both, in the community.

The selling entity for the community must, at least once per year, give each home owner and tenant written notice of the charges payable by the selling entity for the supply of electricity to the parent connection point from which electricity is supplied to each site.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.
The selling entity must review the offer under the selling entity’s contract with the retailer for the supply of electricity to the parent connection point (the supply contract)—
if the current supply contract has a contract period of more than 2 years—before entering into the next supply contract, or
otherwise—at least once every 2 years.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.

However, if the selling entity is both a third party supplier for the community and the retailer supplying electricity to the parent connection point, a review under subsection (3) must be carried out by the operator of the community.

The person carrying out a review under subsection (3) must, for the purposes of ensuring the offer under the supply contract is the best available offer for the embedded network, compare the offer with at least 1 other comparable offer from another retailer.
The person carrying out a review under subsection (3) must, within 30 days of completing the review, give each home owner and tenant written notice of the review, including details of—
the comparable offers considered by the person, and
the outcome of the review.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.
In this section—
selling entity, for a community, means—
if the electricity is sold to home owners or tenants, or both, by a third party supplier for the community—the third party supplier, or
otherwise—the operator of the community.
parent connection point has the same meaning as in the National Electricity Rules.
The operator of a community or a third party supplier may charge a fee for a late or dishonoured payment if—
the payment relates to utility charges payable by a home owner or tenant for the use of electricity, and
the fee is not more than the amount that the operator or third party supplier can charge as a retailer or exempt seller.
The operator may charge a fee for a late or dishonoured payment if—
the payment relates to utility charges payable by a home owner or tenant for the use of a utility other than electricity, and
the fee is not more than the amount that could have been charged if the service was supplied directly to the home owner or tenant by the utility service provider.
The operator or third party supplier may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the home owner or tenant to pay to the operator or third party supplier—
any unpaid utility charge, or
any unpaid fee for late payment, or
any unpaid fee for a dishonoured payment.
The Tribunal may, on application under this section, make—
an order requiring the home owner or tenant to pay the unpaid charge or fee (or a specified part of it) within a specified period, and
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.
The Tribunal may determine the application without conducting a hearing with the consent of the parties.

heading.b: Site fees cannot be used to pay utility charges

block.txt: The operator of a community must not apply any amount paid by a home owner by way of site fees towards payment of other outstanding fees or charges payable by the home owner (not being site fees), unless specifically authorised to do so by this Act.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.
See section 60(2).

heading.b: Separate measurement or metering of supply of utility

block.txt: This section applies if—
the use by the home owner under a site agreement of a utility at the residential site is not separately measured or metered, and
the operator wishes to separately measure or meter the use of the utility at the residential site.
The operator of a community must pay the cost of installing a measuring device or meter to measure the use of the utility at the residential site.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
This section applies if—
the use by the home owner under a site agreement of a utility at the residential site is not separately measured or metered, and
either of the following events (a change event) happens—
the home owner’s use of the utility becomes separately measured or metered and the cost of the use becomes payable by the home owner,
the utility stops being available for use by the home owner for any reason other than the default or neglect of the home owner.
The operator of the community must, within 14 days after the change event happens, give the home owner a notice (a utility cost notice) stating the following—
the utility cost factored into the site fees payable under the agreement and how the utility cost has been worked out,
the date the change event happened,
the site fees payable from that date,
that if the home owner disputes the utility cost, the home owner may, within 30 days after receiving the notice, apply to the Tribunal for an order.
The Tribunal may, on application by the home owner within 30 days after receiving the utility cost notice, make any order the Tribunal considers appropriate in the circumstances.

The site fees payable from the day the change event happens (the change event day) are the site fees payable immediately before the change event day, reduced by the utility cost stated in the utility cost notice.

The operator must, within 14 days after the home owner received the utility cost notice, refund to the home owner any overpayment of site fees, relating to the utility cost, from the change event day.
Maximum penalty (subsection (5)): 10 penalty units.

heading.b: Tribunal review of utility cost and reduction in site fees

block.txt: This section applies if—
the operator under a site agreement contravenes section 81(2), or
the home owner under a site agreement who receives a utility cost notice under section 81(2) disputes the utility cost stated in the notice.
The home owner under the site agreement mentioned in subsection (1)(a) may apply to the Tribunal for an order under subsection (4).
The home owner mentioned in subsection (1)(b) may apply to the Tribunal, within 30 days after receiving the notice, for an order under subsection (4).
On application by the home owner, the Tribunal may make any of the following orders—
an order reducing the site fees payable under the agreement, from the change event day, by the amount the Tribunal considers appropriate,
another order the Tribunal considers appropriate.
An example of an order under subsection (4)(b) is an order that the operator refund to the home owner any overpaid site fees from the change event day.
In making an order under subsection (4), the Tribunal may have regard to the following—
relevant available information about the costs of supplying utilities in the local government area in which the community is situated,
any terms of the site agreement about utility costs,
anything else the Tribunal considers relevant.
The billing entity for a community must comply with the requirements relating to billing for electricity and gas specified in—
if the operator of the community or a third party supplier for the community is a retailer—the National Energy Retail Rules, or
if the operator of the community or a third party supplier for the community is an exempt seller—the AER Exempt Selling Guidelines.
The billing entity for a community must issue a bill to the following person for utility charges payable for the use of a utility, other than electricity and gas, at least once every 3 months—
if the utility charges are payable by, and billed directly to, a tenant in a residential site—the tenant,
otherwise—the home owner required to pay the utility charges.
A bill issued under subsection (2) must include the following—
the home owner’s or tenant’s name,
the operator’s name and trading name, if any,
the operator’s contact details,
the name and address of the community,
the number or other identifier of the residential site,
the number or other identifier of the meter, if any, for the home,
the date of issue,
the date on which payment is due,
the billing period,
the charges, fees and tariffs that apply and how each was calculated, including the following—
the service availability charge,
the number of days in the billing period,
the usage rate,
the total usage charge,
in relation to meter readings or estimates, if applicable—
whether an estimate has been applied, and
the meter reading or estimate, and
the meter reading or estimate for the last bill issued, and
the quantity of the service used, or estimated to have been used, during the billing period,
the amount, if any, deducted or credited under—
a concession, rebate or relief scheme, or
a payment plan,
details of the available payment methods,
a telephone number for the purpose of making a billing enquiry or complaint, if not included in the operator’s contact details.
The billing entity for a community, must give a home owner or tenant reasonable access to utility bills and other documents relating to utility charges payable by the home owner or tenant.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.
In this section—
billing entity, for a community, means—
if utility bills are issued by a third party supplier for the community—the third party supplier, or
if utility bills are issued by another entity on behalf of the operator of the community—the other entity, or
otherwise—the operator of the community.
National Energy Retail Rules has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
National Electricity Rules has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
AER Exempt Selling Guidelines has the same meaning as in the National Energy Retail Law (NSW).
If a home owner or tenant pays for utility charges in person, the person receiving the payment must immediately give the home owner or tenant a receipt that includes the following—
the home owner’s or tenant’s name,
the name and address of the community,
the number or other identifier of the residential site,
the date on which payment was received,
the billing period for which the utility charges are paid,
the amount paid,
the amount, if any, by which the home owner is in debit or credit as at the date of payment.
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.

If a home owner or tenant pays for utility charges in another way and asks for a receipt, the person receiving the payment must, as soon as practicable after receiving the payment, give the home owner or tenant a receipt that includes the information specified in subsection (1)(a)–(g).
Maximum penalty—10 penalty units.

heading.b: Recovery of amounts paid under a mistake of law or fact

block.txt: A home owner or tenant is entitled to recover an amount paid under this Part to the operator of a community or a third party supplier under a mistake of law or fact.

A home owner may, with the consent of the operator of the community, recover an amount mistakenly paid to the operator under this Part by deducting it from site fees payable by the home owner under the site agreement.
The Tribunal may, on application by a home owner, tenant or operator, make an order resolving a dispute concerning the operation of this section in the circumstances of a particular case.

The Minister must review this part to determine whether the policy objectives of the part relating to utility charges for electricity remain valid and whether the provisions of the part remain appropriate for securing the objectives.
In undertaking the review, the Minister may investigate related matters that the Minister considers appropriate.
The review must be undertaken within 3 years of the day this section commences.
A report on the outcome of the review and related investigations must be tabled in each House of Parliament within 4 years of the day this section commences.
Written rules relating to the use, enjoyment, control and management of a community may be made in accordance with this Part.
Without limiting subsection (1), a community rule may be made with respect to any matter specified in the regulations as being a matter that may be the subject of a community rule.
The community rules must be fair and reasonable and must be clearly expressed.
There is a rebuttable presumption that a community rule is not fair and reasonable if it does not apply uniformly to all residents of the community.
A community rule cannot invalidate anything that has already occurred.
A community rule that prohibits a pet does not apply to a pet that is living with a resident of the community when the rule is made and that continues to live there after the rule is made.
A term of a site agreement or tenancy agreement has no effect to the extent the term would—
make all or any part of the community rules part of the agreement, or
be substantially the same (or to the same effect) as a provision of a community rule or any part of a community rule.

A term of a site agreement or tenancy agreement prevails over a provision of the community rules to the extent of any inconsistency. This applies whether the provision of the community rules came into effect before, on or after the date of the agreement.

heading.b: Community rules to be consistent with other laws

block.txt: A community rule is of no effect to the extent that it is inconsistent with this Act or any other Act or law.
The Commissioner may publish model community rules that may be adopted for a community.

The operator of a community may make written community rules for the community if, at the time the rules are made, the community has no residents. This also applies to the proposed operator of a proposed community.
If a community has residents but no community rules, community rules may be made for the community in the same way as community rules may be amended under section 90.
The operator of a community may make written amendments to the community rules.
An amendment does not have effect unless—
each resident has been given written notice of the amendment, and
if the community has a residents committee—the operator has advised and consulted with the committee about the amendment and has done so before giving notice to residents under paragraph (a).
The written notice must be given at least 30 days before the day on which the amendment is to have effect.
On the day that an amendment to the community rules takes effect, the community rules are amended in accordance with the amendment.
See also section 95, which enables the Tribunal to stay the time when an amendment to the community rules takes effect.
For the purposes of this section, an amendment of community rules includes—
a variation or deletion of a rule, and
the addition of a new rule, and
the replacement of a rule with a new rule, including the replacement of all the rules with a new set of rules.
The regulations may prohibit a specified type of community rule.

Without limiting subsection (1), a community rule is of a prohibited type if it requires or has the effect of requiring a home owner to replace or remove an older home, or to make upgrades or improvements to a home, for any reason that is not related to health or safety.
The operator of a community must not make or attempt to enforce a type of community rule that is prohibited by this section.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
A community rule of a type that is prohibited by this section is of no effect.
The residents, owner and operator of a community must comply with the community rules.
Each resident must use reasonable endeavours to ensure compliance with the community rules by—
any occupants living with the resident, and
any other persons who are in the community at the resident’s invitation.
The operator must use reasonable endeavours to ensure compliance with the community rules by—
all residents and occupants, and
any employees of the operator, and
any other persons who are in the community at the operator’s invitation.
The operator of a community must ensure that the community rules are enforced and interpreted consistently and fairly.

The operator of a community may give a notice to a resident to remedy a breach of a community rule within a specified period of at least 30 days. The notice is to be in writing and to be in the approved form (if any).

If it appears to the operator that the breach has not been remedied within the period specified in the notice, the operator may, within a further period of 30 days, apply to the Tribunal for orders under this section.
The Tribunal may, on application under this section and if it considers the breach is in the circumstances sufficient to justify its doing so, make any one or more of the following orders—
an order requiring compliance with the rule within a specified period,
an order terminating the resident’s site agreement or tenancy agreement,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.
In considering the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal may consider (but is not limited to considering) the following—
the nature of the breach,
any previous breaches of the community rules by the resident,
any steps taken by the resident to remedy the breach,
any steps taken by the operator about the breach,
the previous history of the operator or resident so far as it is relevant,
whether the community rule is being enforced and interpreted consistently and fairly.
The Tribunal may refuse to make an order if it is satisfied that the breach has been remedied.

heading.b: Applications to Tribunal by residents for breaches

block.txt: A resident of a community may give a written notice (in the approved form, if any) to the operator to take action for the remedy of a breach of a community rule by any person within a specified period of at least 30 days.

If it appears to the resident that the breach has not been remedied within the 30-day period, the resident may, within a further period of 30 days, apply to the Tribunal for orders under this section.
The Tribunal may, on application under this section and if it considers the breach is in the circumstances sufficient to justify its doing so, make either or both of the following orders—
an order requiring compliance with the rule within a specified period,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.

heading.b: Applications to Tribunal about community rules

block.txt: A resident or operator of a community may apply to the Tribunal if there is a dispute about whether—
a community rule complies with this Part, or
the procedure for making or amending a community rule has been correctly followed.
The Tribunal may, on application under this section, make one or more of the following orders—
an order amending or setting aside the community rule,
an order modifying the operation of the community rule in its application to some of the persons to or in respect of whom the rule applies,
an order upholding the community rule,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.
The Tribunal may make an order staying the time when a community rule takes effect pending its decision whether to make an order under subsection (2).
In this section—
community rule includes—
a proposed community rule, and
an amendment or proposed amendment of a community rule.
The residents of a community may by resolution establish a residents committee.

The resolution must be carried by a majority of residents of the community at a meeting to which all residents of the community have been invited. The meeting is referred to as the establishment meeting.
Section 98 provides for the election of the members of the residents committee at the establishment meeting.
The operator of a community must not—
discourage or prevent the establishment or continued existence of a residents committee, or
require a residents committee to be incorporated or to take out any form of insurance.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.
The functions of a residents committee for a community are—
to represent the interests of the residents, and to consult regularly with residents or the operator or both, in connection with—
the day-to-day running of the community, and
any complaint or proposal about the operation of the community raised by a resident, and
to call meetings of all the residents of the community for the purpose of considering and voting on any matter relating to the community.
The operator of a community must not obstruct the residents committee in the exercise of its functions or prevent it from using community facilities that are generally available to residents.

The operator of a community must, as soon as practicable after being requested to do so by the residents committee, give the committee a list of the names of all current residents of the community, their site numbers and their postal addresses (if different from their site numbers).
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.
The members of a residents committee for a community are to be elected from time to time by residents of the community.
The members are elected by resolution of a majority of residents at the establishment meeting, and thereafter at meetings—
to which all residents have been invited, and
convened by the residents committee (or by residents from at least 5 residential sites in the community, if there are no members for the time being or the members are unwilling or unable to act).
The residents committee can consist only of residents of the community who are at least 18 years old.
A member holds office for a term of not more than one year, but may be re-elected.
The number of members to hold office is to be the number agreed at the establishment meeting or by resolution of a majority of residents from time to time at later meetings.

If the number of eligible persons currently nominated for election does not exceed the number of vacancies, the chairperson for the meeting is to declare the nominated persons duly elected, and they are members without the need for taking votes or other action.
A residents committee may elect a chairperson or secretary, or both, from among its members.
An office holder—
holds office until his or her current term as a member of the committee ends, but may be re-elected, and
may be removed from office, at any time, by resolution of the committee.
Removal from office under this section does not of itself affect the former office holder’s membership of the committee.
A residents committee may—
determine its own procedures, and
form subcommittees and determine each subcommittee’s procedures.
A residents committee may adopt and vary a constitution by resolution of the committee.
The Commissioner may publish a model constitution that may be adopted by a residents committee.

heading.b: No more than one residents committee for a community

block.txt: There can be no more than one residents committee for a community at any time.

If more than one body or committee (regardless of its name) purports to be the residents committee for a particular community, the operator or a resident may apply to the Tribunal for (and the Tribunal may make) an order determining which body or committee (if any) is the residents committee for the community.
Nothing in this Part prevents the residents of a community from establishing other committees for other purposes (for example, a social club).

Nothing in this Part prevents the residents committee and the operator from establishing and maintaining a consultative joint committee. However, a joint committee continues to exist only while there is a residents committee.

heading.b: Residents’ rights to membership of organisations

block.txt: A resident of a community has a right to be a member of—
the residents committee, or
an external communities organisation if the resident is eligible to be a member of the organisation.
A representative of an external communities organisation has a right of reasonable access to a community to consult with residents of the community.
A person must not unreasonably interfere with a person’s rights under this section.
Maximum penalty—20 penalty units.
In this section—
external communities organisation means an organisation that represents the interests of residents of communities generally or of 2 or more communities within a particular locality.

heading.b: Relationship of operator with residents committee

block.txt: None of the following people can be members of a residents committee—
the operator of the community,
a close associate of the operator (even if he or she is a resident).
The operator of a community or close associate of the operator may, if invited by the residents committee, attend and speak at—
a meeting of the committee or of a subcommittee, or
a meeting of residents convened by the committee.

This Part applies to a home owned by a home owner or former home owner that is located on a residential site in a community. Accordingly, references in this Part to a home owner include former home owners.
The definition of home owner in section 4 provides that the term includes an executor, administrator or beneficiary of the estate of a deceased home owner.
Nothing in this Part applies to the sale of a home that is not located in a community.

heading.b: Rights and obligations regarding sale of homes
Right to sell home on residential site

block.txt: A home owner is entitled to sell the home while the home is located on the residential site.
The home owner is required to give the operator of the community a notice of intention to offer the home for sale before offering it for sale.
A notice is taken to have lapsed—
if the home owner notifies the operator that the home owner no longer intends to offer the home for sale, or
if 3 months have passed since the notice was given and—
the home is not being advertised for sale, or
there is no selling agent for the sale of the home.
A home owner is entitled to display a “for sale” sign in or on the home, but only if the home owner first informs the operator of the community of the intention to offer the home for sale.
A home owner is not entitled to display a “for sale” sign anywhere else in the community without the consent of the operator.

heading.b: Interference with right to sell home

block.txt: The operator of a community must not cause or permit any interference with, or any attempt to interfere with—
a home owner’s right to sell a home, or
a home owner’s right to display a “for sale” sign in or on a home.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.
Without limiting subsection (1)—
interference with a home owner’s right includes hindering the exercise of the right, and
interference with a home owner’s right to sell a home includes unreasonably restricting prospective home owners from inspecting the home or any common area of the community, and
interference includes making false or misleading statements about the community that affect or may affect either right, and

interference includes taking any action to require the home owner to comply with any requirement made by or under the Local Government Act 1993 after becoming aware that the home owner is seeking to sell his or her home (unless the matter has been the subject of previous action).
An operator does not interfere with the right to sell the home if the operator declines to enter into a site agreement with a prospective home owner and does so on reasonable grounds.
Without limiting subsection (3), reasonable grounds can be established on—

the basis of unfavourable information about the prospective home owner contained in a residential tenancy database referred to in the Residential Tenancies Act 2010, other than a database referred to in section 210 of that Act, or
the basis that the prospective home owner has been evicted from the community or another community within the past 5 years for a breach of a site agreement by the prospective home owner.

heading.b: Referral of prospective home owner to operator

block.txt: A home owner must ensure that a genuine prospective home owner of the home is advised to contact the operator of the community about the proposed sale before a contract for the sale of the home is entered into, unless the home owner is aware that contact has already been made.
This section helps the operator to comply with the disclosure obligations under Part 4.
A contract of sale or site agreement is not invalidated by a partial or complete failure of—
the home owner to comply with subsection (1), or
the prospective home owner to contact the operator as contemplated by that subsection or to continue contact, or
the operator to respond to contact from a prospective home owner as contemplated by that subsection.

heading.b: Operator to enter new site agreement

block.txt: This section applies if a purchaser or prospective home owner under a contract, or proposed contract, for the sale of the home (the sale contract) requests the operator of the community to enter into a new site agreement (the new site agreement) for the residential site with the purchaser or prospective home owner.
This section is not relevant if the purchaser or prospective home owner intends to remove the home from the community.
The operator must enter into the new site agreement after the request is made, unless—

the operator declines to enter into the agreement and does so on reasonable grounds (including, for example, the ground that it appears reasonably unlikely that the sale contract will be entered into), or
without limiting paragraph (a), the operator and the purchaser or prospective home owner do not agree on the terms of the proposed agreement.
If the sale contract is entered into before the new site agreement is entered into—
the contract may include a term to the effect that the contract is subject to the new site agreement being entered into within a specified period after the contract is entered into, and
the contract is unenforceable if it includes that term and the new site agreement is not entered into within that period.
If the new site agreement is entered into before the sale contract is entered into—
the agreement may include a term to the effect that the agreement is subject to the sale contract being entered into within a specified period after the agreement is entered into, and
the agreement is unenforceable if it includes that term and the sale contract is not entered into within that period.
The site fees under the new site agreement must not exceed fair market value.
Fair market value is the higher of the following—
the site fees currently payable by the home owner who is selling the home,
the site fees currently payable for residential sites of a similar size and location within the same community.
The operator must not unreasonably delay or refuse to enter into a new site agreement referred to in subsection (2).
A home owner may appoint the operator of the community or another person as a selling agent to sell, or to negotiate the sale of, the home.
An operator cannot require a home owner—
to appoint the operator or any other person as selling agent, or
to use the services of the operator or any other person,
in connection with the sale or negotiation of the sale of the home, either under the terms of the site agreement or otherwise. Such a requirement is unenforceable.
If the home owner appoints a person other than the operator as selling agent, the operator must not unreasonably hinder the appointed person’s access to the community.
Maximum penalty—50 penalty units.
When the operator acts as a selling agent, the operator is not required to hold—
a licence as agent under the Property and Stock Agents Act 2002, or
a motor dealer’s licence under the Motor Dealers and Repairers Act 2013.
Neither a sale commission nor incidental expenses are payable in connection with the sale of a home, unless—
there is a written selling agency agreement between the home owner and the selling agent entered before the sale, and
if a sale commission is to be payable—the agreement—
provides for the payment of the commission, and
specifies the amount of the sale commission or the method of its calculation, and
sets out the services the agent will perform in return for payment of the sale commission, and
if incidental expenses are to be payable—the agreement—
provides for the payment of the expenses, and
sets out the nature of the services for which the expenses will be payable, and
an invoice or statement of claim is provided to the home owner, setting out amounts claimed and details of the services performed.
No sale commission is payable if—
the home is not sold, or
the home is sold but the services provided by the selling agent are not the effective cause of the sale, or
the home is sold but the purchaser is the operator or a close associate of the operator.
In this section—

incidental expenses means reasonable expenses that are incurred by the selling agent in connection with the sale or negotiation of the sale of a home and paid or payable to another person who provides an advertising or other service, and includes anything of a kind prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this definition.
sale commission means a commission, fee or other amount (other than incidental expenses) for the sale or negotiation of the sale of a home.

heading.b: Operator to hold money in trust

block.txt: When the operator of a community receives any money under a selling agency agreement (except sale commission payable to the operator under the agreement), the operator holds the money in trust and must—
deposit the money, as soon as possible but within 7 days after receiving it, in an ADI account that is—
used only for depositing money under selling agency agreements, and
opened in the name of the operator, and
entitled “sales trust account”, and
when the sale is completed, pay the proceeds at the direction of the home owner, after deducting—
any amounts owing to the operator by way of expenses or commission under the selling agency agreement, and
any other fees and charges owing to the operator under the site agreement.
The Interpretation Act 1987 defines an ADI as an authorised deposit-taking institution within the meaning of the Banking Act 1959 of the Commonwealth.

A home owner, prospective home owner, operator or selling agent may apply to the Tribunal for the resolution of any dispute concerning the sale of the home, the terms of the proposed site agreement or the proposed site fees, in particular—
any dispute about compliance with a provision of this Part, and
any dispute about whether a sale commission, incidental expense or other fee or charge is payable to the operator or agent in relation to the sale of the home, and

any dispute about the amount of a sale commission, incidental expense or other fee or charge payable or paid to the operator or agent in relation to the sale of the home (including a claim that a sale commission is excessive when compared to sale commissions charged by local real estate agents), and
any dispute about interference by the operator or another person with the sale of the home, and
any dispute about the reasonableness of a decision by the operator not to enter into a site agreement with a purchaser or prospective home owner.
The Tribunal may make the following orders—
an order that the home owner or prospective home owner pay a sale commission, incidental expense or other fee or charge of a specified amount to the operator or selling agent,
an order reducing the amount of sale commission, incidental expense or other fee or charge payable by a home owner or prospective home owner to the operator or selling agent,

an order that the operator or selling agent refund any sale commission, incidental expense or other fee or charge paid by the home owner or prospective home owner to the operator or selling agent (or any part of such a commission, expense, fee or charge),
an order preventing interference with the sale of the home,
an order requiring the operator to take all necessary steps to facilitate the sale of the home to a specified prospective home owner,
an order that the operator pay compensation where—
there is or has been interference by the operator with the sale, whether by action or inaction, or
the operator refuses to enter into a new site agreement without reasonable grounds,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.

Without limiting its powers, the Tribunal may dismiss an application by the home owner for compensation under subsection (2)(f)(ii) if the Tribunal is satisfied that the grounds on which the operator declined to enter into a site agreement with a prospective home owner were reasonable.
A site agreement terminates only in one or more of the following circumstances—
if either party gives the other party a termination notice in accordance with this Part and the home owner delivers up vacant possession of the residential site after the notice is given,
if the Tribunal makes a termination order for the agreement and the home owner delivers up vacant possession of the residential site or a warrant for possession is enforced,
if the home owner delivers up vacant possession of the residential site with the prior consent of the operator, whether or not the consent is later withdrawn,
if the home owner agrees to relocation to a different residential site and a new site agreement is entered into under section 135,
if the Tribunal makes an order declaring that the home owner abandoned the residential site,
if the occupation of the home is given over to another person following the completion of the sale of the home to the operator or another person.
The home owner under a site agreement may give a termination notice without having to specify a ground for termination.
The notice must specify the day, not earlier than 30 days after the notice is given, that the agreement is terminated.
The home owner must give the operator vacant possession of the residential site on or before the stated day.
The operator of a community under a site agreement may give the home owner a termination notice for the termination of the agreement, but only in accordance with this Part.
A termination notice must be in the approved form, be signed by the operator or a person acting on behalf of the operator, and set out the following matters—
the residential site concerned,
the day on which vacant possession of the residential site is to be given,
the ground for the notice.
A termination notice that does not comply with this section is of no effect.
The party who gives a termination notice may, at any time, revoke the notice with the consent of the other party.
The Tribunal may make a termination order for a site agreement even if there is a defect in the notice or the manner of service of the notice if—
it thinks it appropriate to do so in the circumstances of the case, and

it is satisfied that the person to whom the notice was given has not suffered any disadvantage because of the defect in the notice or service or that any disadvantage has been overcome by the order and any associated order.
The Tribunal may, on application by a party to a site agreement, make any of the following orders—
an order resolving a dispute about a termination notice,
an order declaring that a termination notice was or was not given in accordance with this Part,
any ancillary order that the Tribunal, in the circumstances, thinks appropriate.

heading.b: Circumstances in which operator can initiate termination
Termination by operator for breach of agreement

block.txt: The operator of a community may give a termination notice on the ground that the home owner has seriously or persistently breached the site agreement.
The termination notice must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than 90 days after the day on which the notice is given.
The termination notice may specify a date for vacating the residential site that is before the end of the fixed term of the site agreement if it is a fixed term agreement.
For the purposes of this section, the home owner is not in breach of the site agreement for non-payment of a site fee unless the fee has remained unpaid for at least 30 days.
The Tribunal may make a termination order if it is satisfied that—
a termination notice was given under this section and the home owner has not vacated the residential site as required by the notice, and
the home owner has breached the site agreement, and
the breach is, in the circumstances of the case, sufficient to justify termination of the agreement.
In considering the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal may consider (but is not limited to considering) the following—
the nature of the breach,
any previous breaches,
any steps taken by the home owner to remedy the breach,
any steps taken by the operator of the community about the breach,
the previous history of the home owner’s occupation of the residential site.
The Tribunal may refuse to make the termination order if it is satisfied that the home owner has remedied the breach.

heading.b: Termination by operator for repairs and upgrading

block.txt: The operator of a community may give a termination notice on the ground that the operator requires vacant possession of the residential site in order to comply with an obligation imposed by or under an Act to carry out works (including works in the nature of repairs or upgrading) within the residential site or the community.
The termination notice must be accompanied by a copy of any order or notice imposing the obligation.
The termination notice must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than 90 days after the day on which the notice is given.
The Tribunal may, on application by the home owner, make an order settling any dispute as to whether vacant possession is necessary in order to comply with the obligation.
The termination notice is of no effect if the notice does not comply with this section or if the Tribunal determines that vacant possession is not necessary in order to comply with the obligation.
The operator of a community may give a termination notice on the ground that the community is to be closed and used by the operator or another person for a purpose other than a residential community.

If use of the community for the new purpose requires development consent under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, the termination notice must not be given unless development consent for the proposed use has been obtained under that Act.
The operator must give at least 7 days’ notice to the Commissioner before giving a termination notice on a ground referred to in this section.
Maximum penalty—50 penalty units.
Giving this notice may assist with providing an assistance protocol for closure of a community.
A failure to comply with subsection (3) does not invalidate a termination notice.
The termination notice must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than—
12 months after the day on which the notice is given, or
in the case of an agreement for a fixed term, the day following the date on which the fixed term ends,
whichever is the later.
The home owner may, within 90 days after receiving a notice specifying a date for vacating the residential site, apply to the Tribunal for an order postponing the date.

Unless the home owner advises the operator in writing that the operator’s assistance under this subsection is not required, the operator is, after giving the termination notice, required to use reasonable endeavours to obtain (or make available) for the home owner alternative accommodation that—
is of approximately the same standard as, and requires no greater financial outlay on the part of the home owner than, the home owner’s current residential site, and
is acceptable to the home owner or reasonably ought to be acceptable to the home owner.

Without otherwise limiting the Tribunal’s powers to make a termination order in connection with the termination notice, the Tribunal is required to take into account the endeavours used by the operator to obtain (or make available) alternative accommodation for the home owner.

heading.b: Termination by operator for change in use of residential site

block.txt: The operator of a community may give a termination notice for a particular residential site on the ground that there is to be a change in use of the site.
A termination notice may not be given under this section unless—
the Tribunal has authorised the operator to give a termination notice because of the proposed change of use of the residential site, and
if the change of use requires development consent under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979, development consent for the proposed use has been obtained under that Act.

The Tribunal may, on application by the operator of a community, make an order authorising the operator to give a termination notice in respect of a site agreement because of a proposed change of use of the residential site to which the agreement relates.
The Tribunal is not to authorise the giving of a termination notice under this section if—
the change of use is not proposed in good faith, or
the change of use would permit use of the residential site in connection with an agreement or arrangement referred to in section 7.
A termination notice given under this section must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than—
12 months after the day on which the notice is given, or
in the case of an agreement for a fixed term—the day following the date on which the fixed term ends,
whichever is the later.
The home owner may, within 90 days after receiving a notice specifying a date for vacating the residential site, apply to the Tribunal for an order postponing the date.

Unless the home owner advises the operator in writing that the operator’s assistance under this subsection is not required, the operator is, after giving the termination notice, required to use reasonable endeavours to obtain (or make available) for the home owner alternative accommodation that—
is of approximately the same standard as, and requires no greater financial outlay on the part of the home owner than, the home owner’s current residential site, and
is acceptable to the home owner or reasonably ought to be acceptable to the home owner.

Without otherwise limiting the Tribunal’s powers to make a termination order in connection with the termination notice, the Tribunal is required to take into account the endeavours used by the operator to obtain (or make available) alternative accommodation for the home owner.

heading.b: Termination by operator for compulsory acquisition

block.txt: The operator of a community may give a termination notice on the ground that the residential site is appropriated or acquired under an Act of the State or the Commonwealth by compulsory process authorised by that Act.
The termination notice must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than 90 days after the day on which the notice is given.
The home owner whose site agreement is terminated under this section is entitled to be paid compensation in accordance with Division 6.

heading.b: Termination by operator for lack of authority for use of residential site

block.txt: The operator of a community may give a termination notice on the ground that the residential site is not lawfully useable for the purposes of a residential site.
For example, a notice may be given if the home owner is occupying a short term site on a permanent basis in contravention of a requirement made under the Local Government Act 1993.
The termination notice must not specify a date for vacating the residential site that is earlier than 120 days after the day on which the notice is given.
A home owner whose site agreement is terminated under this section is entitled to be paid compensation in accordance with Division 6 if the residential site—
was, unknown to the home owner, not lawfully useable for the purposes of a residential site at the time the agreement was entered into, or
became, through some action of the operator of the community after the agreement was entered into, not lawfully useable for the purposes of a residential site.

heading.b: Application by operator for termination for serious misconduct

block.txt: The operator of a community may apply to the Tribunal for a termination order on the ground of serious misconduct, without the need for a termination notice to be given.

The Tribunal may make the termination order under Division 3 if it is satisfied that a home owner (or any person who is occupying or jointly occupying the residential site) has intentionally or recklessly caused or permitted—
serious damage to any property in the community, or
injury to any person when lawfully present in the community, or
the residential site to be used for any purpose that is illegal at common law or under an Act, or
the operator (or the operator’s agent or an employee or contractor of the operator or operator’s agent) or any resident to be seriously or persistently threatened or abused.
The termination order may take effect before or after the end of the fixed term if the site agreement is for a fixed term.
The Tribunal may, on application by the operator of a community, make a termination order in accordance with this Division.
A termination order may be made either—
if vacant possession of a residential site is not given by the specified date as required by a termination notice, or
if an application for the order can be made under this Part without the need for a termination notice.

If the Tribunal makes a termination order, it must also make an order for possession of the residential site (a possession order) specifying the day on which the possession order takes or took effect.

The Tribunal may suspend the operation of a possession order if it is satisfied that it is desirable to do so, having regard to the relative hardship likely to be caused to the operator and home owner by the suspension.

heading.b: Prohibition on certain recovery proceedings in courts

block.txt: The owner or operator of a community must not commence proceedings against a home owner in the Supreme Court, the District Court or the Local Court to obtain recovery of possession of a residential site subject to a site agreement.

heading.b: Recovery of possession of residential site prohibited except by order

block.txt: A person must not enter a residential site, or a home on a residential site, for the purpose of taking possession of the site or home before or after the end of a site agreement unless—
the person is acting in accordance with a warrant arising out of a possession order of the Tribunal or a writ or warrant arising out of a judgment or order of a court, or
the home owner has given vacant possession of the residential site, or
the Tribunal has made an order declaring that the home owner has abandoned the residential site.
Maximum penalty—200 penalty units.
Under Division 7 an operator may apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring that a home owner has abandoned a residential site.

A court that finds an offence under this section proven may, in addition to any other penalty it may impose, order that compensation be paid to the home owner by the person who committed the offence or on whose behalf the offence was committed.
This section applies to a person who enters a residential site, or a home on a residential site, on his or her own behalf or on behalf of another person.

The principal registrar of the Tribunal may, on the application of an operator in whose favour a possession order was made, issue a warrant for possession of the residential site concerned if the principal registrar is satisfied that the order or a condition of suspension of the order has not been complied with.

An application for a warrant for possession may be made immediately, if the possession order so provides, or not more than 30 days after the date by which vacant possession was required or within such further period as the Tribunal may permit.

Without limiting subsection (2), the Tribunal may permit an application to be made within a further period if the delay in making the application is attributable to genuine attempts by the applicant to arrange for breaches of the site agreement or this Act to be remedied so as to enable the continued occupation of the residential site under the site agreement.
A warrant for possession is to be in the form approved by the principal registrar of the Tribunal and must authorise a sheriff’s officer—
to enter a specified residential site, or a home or any part of a home on a residential site, and to give possession of the residential site to the person specified in the warrant, and
to remove the occupants of the residential site, or a home on the residential site, from the community and prevent their access to the community.
Section 7A of the Sheriff Act 2005 contains provisions relating to the enforcement of warrants.
The provisions of section 7A(1) and (2) of the Sheriff Act 2005 extend to authorising a sheriff’s officer executing a warrant for possession to do the things referred to in subsection (4)(b).

heading.b: Relocation of home owner by agreement

block.txt: The operator and a home owner under a site agreement may agree to the relocation of the home owner to a different residential site, whether within the same community or within another community with the same operator.
All reasonable costs of relocating the home owner under the agreement are payable by the party initiating the proposal to relocate, unless the parties otherwise agree.
A person must not coerce or attempt to coerce a home owner into—
relocating to a different residential site, or
agreeing to relocate to a different residential site.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.

If the home owner agrees to the relocation, a new site agreement is to be entered into, with the same or substantially the same terms and conditions as the previous site agreement, and the previous site agreement is terminated. The site fees payable under the new site agreement may be reduced, but may not be increased, by reason of the relocation.

heading.b: Relocation of home owner by operator’s request

block.txt: As an alternative to issuing a termination notice under Division 2, the operator may, by notice in writing, request the home owner to relocate the home to a different residential site on or by a specified date, whether within the same community or within another community within a reasonable distance and with the same operator.
The specified date must not be earlier than 90 days after the notice is given.
If the home owner agrees to the relocation, the costs of relocating the home under this section are payable by the operator.

If the home owner agrees to the relocation, a new site agreement is to be entered into, with the same or substantially the same terms and conditions as the previous site agreement, and the previous site agreement is terminated. The site fees payable under the new site agreement may be reduced, but may not be increased, by reason of the relocation.
If the home owner advises the operator that the home owner does not agree to the relocation or the notice expires (whichever first occurs), the operator may elect to issue a termination notice.

heading.b: Purchase of home by owner or operator of community

block.txt: Nothing in this Part prevents the owner or operator of a community from offering to buy a home in the community and the home owner agreeing to sell the home to the owner or operator of the community for an agreed price.

heading.b: Tribunal may value homes to facilitate sale

block.txt: The purpose of this section is to enable the Tribunal to assist an owner or operator of a community and a home owner to come to an agreement as to the value of the home owner’s home where there is a proposed sale of the home from the home owner to the owner or operator of the community.

The Tribunal may, on application by the owner or operator of the community or the home owner (or both), make an order determining the value of the home. For that purpose, the Tribunal may obtain a valuation of the home, or seek advice as to the valuation of the home, from one or more qualified valuers.
Any costs payable to a qualified valuer are payable in such proportions as are agreed between the parties or (failing agreement) as ordered by the Tribunal.

The Tribunal’s determination of the value of the home is advisory only and does not bind the owner or operator of the community or the home owner or affect any agreement between them for the sale of the home (unless the agreement provides otherwise).
Subject to the regulations, a reference in this section to a qualified valuer is a reference to a person who—
has membership of the Australian Valuers Institute (other than associate or student membership), or
has membership of the Australian Property Institute (other than student or provisional membership), acquired in connection with his or her occupation as a valuer, or
has membership of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors as a chartered valuer, or
is of a class prescribed by the regulations.
This Division applies where an operator gives a termination notice to a home owner, unless it is given under section 122 (for breach of agreement) or 129 (for serious misconduct).

This section applies if, after and in consequence of receiving a termination notice given by an operator (the first operator), a home owner decides to relocate to another community and the other community is operated by a different operator.
The first operator is liable—
to pay in advance the likely reasonable costs of the following—
removing the home from the old residential site (including the costs of disconnecting any services),
transporting the home, and the possessions of its occupants, to the new residential site,
installing the home at the new residential site (including the costs of connecting to the available services),
repairing any damage to the home arising from its relocation,
landscaping the new residential site so as to bring it up to the condition of the old residential site, and
to pay any additional reasonable costs incurred for those purposes after the relocation is complete.
The costs are payable to or at the direction of the person who was the home owner who received the termination notice.
The Tribunal may, on application by a home owner or operator, make an order resolving a dispute concerning the operation of this section in the circumstances of a particular case.

The operator of a community is liable to pay compensation to a home owner as provided for by this section if the operator gives a termination notice to the home owner and the home owner does not want to relocate to another community or is unable to relocate to another community.

If the site agreement specifies any compensation amount or method for determining compensation in the circumstances to which this section applies, the compensation payable is to be determined as specified in the agreement.

If the site agreement does not specify the manner for determining the compensation payable in the circumstances to which this section applies, the following compensation is payable (in advance of relocation)—
compensation for the loss of residency,
compensation for relocation.
The compensation payable for the loss of residency is such amount as is reasonable having regard to the following—
the length of time remaining for the duration (if any) of the site agreement,

the original purchase price paid by the home owner for the home and (if the home was purchased from the owner or operator of the community) any arrangements that were entered into in connection with the purchase,
the current on-site market value of the home (determined as if the termination were not to occur),
site fees payable for the residential site,
any other relevant factor raised by the parties or prescribed by the regulations.
The compensation payable for relocation is such amount as is reasonable determined having regard to the following—
the cost of moving,
inconvenience to the home owner,
the length of time that the occupant or occupants of the home have lived on the residential site,
any other relevant factor raised by the parties or prescribed by the regulations.
If the home owner intends to keep the home—
any amount the home owner is capable of recouping by selling the home off-site is to be deducted from the compensation payable for the loss of residency, and
regard is to be had to the cost of removing and transporting the home in determining the cost of moving (and the compensation payable for relocation).

If the home owner does not intend to keep the home, the home owner must, in return for the payment of compensation under this section, transfer the home (free of all encumbrances) to the operator of the community.
The Tribunal may, on application by a home owner or operator, make an order resolving a dispute concerning the operation of this section in the circumstances of a particular case.
This section does not apply—
in the circumstances to which section 140 applies, or
to arrangements made for the purposes of the sale of a home to the owner or operator of the community.
